title: The last lighthouse keeper on Gull Rock
excerpt: For 31 years, Tomas Varga climbed 112 steps every night. Then the light went automatic.
textContent:
At dusk, Tomas Varga still climbs the 112 iron steps of the Gull Rock lighthouse, even though nobody needs him to anymore. He stops on the 80th step, the way he always has, to look through the porthole at the tide.

"My knees know the count better than I do," he says, laughing, his hand on the cold rail.

Varga arrived on the island in 1994 with two suitcases and a radio. The keeper before him, a gruff fisherman named Ilse Brandt, gave him one piece of advice: never trust a calm sea in October. That winter, a freighter lost its engine a mile offshore, and Varga kept the lamp turning by hand for 14 hours while the coast guard towed it clear.

Last spring, the maritime authority replaced the lamp with an automatic LED beacon that runs on solar panels. Varga's job ended on a Tuesday, by email.

He stayed anyway. He rents the keeper's cottage now, for a symbolic one euro a year, and gives tours to the schoolchildren who come over on the Thursday ferry. He shows them the old brass lens, the logbooks, and the scorch mark on the floor from a kerosene spill in 1997.

On the walk back down, he pauses at the 80th step again. "The light doesn't need me," he says. "But somebody should still be watching the water."
